methodology: 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories
readme: Every record carries a provenance class. 'ipcc' values were read directly from the cited table of the 2006 IPCC Guidelines. 'external' values come from outside the Guidelines and must name their own source. 'assumed' values are our own simplifications. Nothing in this file may be treated as verified unless verified is true.

provenance_classes.ipcc: Read directly from a named table of the 2006 IPCC Guidelines.
provenance_classes.external: Sourced outside the Guidelines. Must be labelled as such in the UI.
provenance_classes.assumed: Our own estimate or simplification. Must be labelled as such in the UI.

conversion_provenance_classes.exact: A defined relationship between two units. Adds no uncertainty, because a definition is not a measurement and cannot be revised by a better source.
conversion_provenance_classes.ipcc_approximate: An approximation the 2006 IPCC Guidelines themselves offer. It is a rule of thumb, not a measured factor, and the Guidelines do not quantify how wrong it can be.
conversion_provenance_classes.user_provided: A figure the user supplied. The engine applies it exactly as given and records that it could not evaluate its uncertainty.

conversion_provenance_note: Unit conversions carry their own three classes and must never be shown using the parameter classes above. A converted quantity is not an emission parameter: nothing in 'units' was measured, and 'exact' is a stronger claim than 'ipcc' rather than a weaker one. Showing a defined conversion as 'assumed', or a user's own density as 'external', would both misdescribe it.

uncertainty_convention.interval: 95 percent confidence interval as published by the IPCC
uncertainty_convention.note: Several IPCC intervals are asymmetric about the default value. Where the engine treats them as symmetric for Approach 1 error propagation (Vol 1 Ch 3 Eq 3.1 and 3.2), it must flag that simplification in the audit trail.
uncertainty_convention.method_multiplication: U_total = sqrt(U1^2 + U2^2 + ... + Un^2)  [Vol 1 Ch 3, Eq 3.1]
uncertainty_convention.method_addition: U_total = sqrt(sum((Ui * xi)^2)) / sum(xi)  [Vol 1 Ch 3, Eq 3.2]

units_note: The units a user may enter a quantity in, and the defined factor that takes each one to the engine's canonical unit for its kind: kilograms for mass, cubic metres for volume, terajoules for energy, and kilograms per cubic metre for density. Every factor here is exact, because every one of them is a definition. Gallons and therms are deliberately absent: the US and imperial gallon differ by about 20 percent and the therm has more than one definition, so offering either would let a user enter a number that means something different from what they think it means.

units.label: Kilograms
units.source: SI base unit of mass. This is the engine's canonical unit, so nothing is converted.

units.label: Tonnes
units.source: Definition of the tonne (metric ton), accepted for use with the SI: 1 t = 10^3 kg.

units.label: Pounds
units.source: International yard and pound agreement (1959): 1 lb = 0.45359237 kg, exactly and by definition.
units.note: The avoirdupois pound. Exact, not rounded: the 1959 agreement defines the pound in terms of the kilogram rather than measuring it.

units.label: Litres
units.source: Definition of the litre, accepted for use with the SI: 1 L = 1 dm^3 = 10^-3 m^3.
units.note: A volume of fuel is only a quantity of fuel at a stated temperature. Warm fuel occupies more space than cold fuel, so the density you supply should be quoted at the same conditions as the volume you are entering.

units.label: Cubic metres
units.source: SI unit of volume. This is the engine's canonical unit, so nothing is converted.
units.note: For a gas, a cubic metre is only a quantity of fuel at a stated temperature and pressure. Meters and bills state the reference conditions they use; the density you supply should be quoted at the same ones.

units.label: Cubic feet
units.source: Derived from the international foot, defined as exactly 0.3048 m (1959): 0.3048^3 = 0.028316846592 m^3, exactly.
units.note: The conversion from cubic feet to cubic metres is geometric and exact. The reference conditions are not: a cubic foot of gas is a different quantity of fuel at different temperatures and pressures, and gas meters marked in cubic feet do not all use the same basis. This engine does not convert between reference conditions and assumes none on your behalf — the conditions are carried entirely by the density you supply, which must be quoted on the same basis as your meter reading.

units.label: Kilowatt-hours
units.source: Definition: 1 W = 1 J/s and 1 h = 3600 s, so 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ exactly, and 1 TJ = 10^6 MJ.

units.label: Kilograms per litre
units.source: Follows from the definition of the litre: 1 m^3 = 10^3 L, so 1 kg/L = 10^3 kg/m^3.

units.label: Kilograms per cubic metre
units.source: SI-coherent unit of density. This is the engine's canonical unit, so nothing is converted.

calorific_basis_note: The net calorific values and emission factors in this library are on a net (lower) heating value basis, which is what the 2006 IPCC Guidelines work in. Energy figures printed on bills and meters are sometimes gross (higher heating value) instead, and the difference is not negligible. Vol 2 Ch 1 of the Guidelines offers a rule of thumb: the net calorific value is about 5 percent below the gross for coal and oil, and about 10 percent below for most natural and manufactured gases. Box 1.1 of the same chapter gives an exact algorithm for the conversion, but it needs fuel analysis data — hydrogen and moisture content — that no household user will have, which is why the rule of thumb is what this calculator can offer. It is an approximation and every figure derived through it is flagged as one. There is no published rule of thumb for solid biomass, so none is applied to charcoal or firewood: their gross-to-net difference is driven by moisture content and is both larger and more variable than 5 percent.

calorific_basis_conversions.label: Gross to net calorific value, coal and oil
calorific_basis_conversions.note: Approximate. Vol 2 Ch 1 Box 1.1 gives an exact algorithm for converting between gross and net calorific values, but it requires fuel analysis data the user will not have. Cited at chapter level: the exact section has not yet been confirmed against the primary text, which is why this record is not verified.

calorific_basis_conversions.label: Gross to net calorific value, natural and manufactured gas
calorific_basis_conversions.note: Approximate, and stated by the Guidelines as covering most such gases rather than all of them. Vol 2 Ch 1 Box 1.1 gives an exact algorithm requiring fuel analysis data the user will not have. Cited at chapter level: the exact section has not yet been confirmed against the primary text, which is why this record is not verified.

categories.1A4b: Energy > Fuel combustion > Other sectors > Residential
categories.1A3b: Energy > Fuel combustion > Transport > Road transportation

fuels.label: Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG)
fuels.calorific_basis_family_note: Vol 2 Ch 1 Table 1.1 classifies liquefied petroleum gases under liquid fuels, not gaseous fuels, so the 5 percent rule for coal and oil is the one that applies rather than the 10 percent rule for natural and manufactured gas. LPG is a gas at ambient pressure, so this is worth a reviewer's eye; see open_questions.

presets.label: 12.5 kg cylinder
presets.note: Assumes one full cylinder. A cylinder is named by the mass of gas it holds when full, so a part-used one holds less than its name. Edit the kilograms if yours was not full.

presets.label: 6 kg cylinder
presets.note: Assumes one full cylinder. Edit the kilograms if yours was not full.

presets.label: 3 kg cylinder
presets.note: Assumes one full cylinder. Edit the kilograms if yours was not full.

fuels.label: Charcoal
fuels.note: Bag weights vary widely by market, so no bag preset is offered; see open_questions. No gross-to-net calorific approximation is published for solid biomass, so an energy figure for charcoal must be entered on a net basis.

fuels.label: Firewood / wood waste
fuels.note: Moisture content drives the very wide NCV interval (7.9 to 31.0 TJ/Gg). Expect large uncertainty and say so in the UI. Moisture is also why no gross-to-net calorific approximation is published for it: the difference is larger and more variable than the 5 percent rule for coal and oil.

fuels.label: Natural gas
fuels.note: Defaults to the kilowatt-hour because that is what a gas bill states. Entering energy skips the calorific value altogether, which is why natural gas is usable without the density this record is otherwise blocked by.

emission_factors.note: Includes carbon oxidation factor of 1 (Vol 2 Ch 2, Eq 2.1).

emission_factors.memo_reason: Biomass CO2. Vol 2 Ch 2 states emissions from combustion of biofuels are reported as information items and are NOT included in sectoral or national totals, to avoid double counting with the AFOLU sector. Display separately; exclude from the headline total.

emission_factors.note: Vol 2 Ch 2: CH4 and N2O from biomass ARE included in sector and national totals, because their effect is additional to the AFOLU stock changes.

emission_factors.memo_reason: Biomass CO2. See charcoal CO2 record.

emission_factors.note: Assumes 100 percent oxidation of fuel carbon (Vol 2 Ch 3).
Table 3.2.2 note (b): if motorcycles are a significant share of the fleet, this default should be adjusted downwards. That adjustment would be an 'assumed' value, not an IPCC one.
Table 3.2.2 note (e): derived from a European heavy duty diesel truck.

Table 3.2.2 states uncertainty ranges have not been provided for LPG. The UI must show 'range not published' rather than inventing one, and the engine must exclude this term from Approach 1 propagation while flagging the omission.
Uncertainty range not published. See LPG CH4 record.

densities_note: Every density here is still null and still unsourced. What changed is what that now means: the calculator no longer refuses volume input outright, it asks the user for the density instead and labels the result as resting on a figure they supplied. A null value here means the engine has no density to fall back on and must ask — it does not mean the engine may guess one. The 'unit' field is the unit the density prompt is offered in for that fuel, because it is the one the fuel's own suppliers quote.

densities.blocking: No default density for petrol. Volume input works only from a density the user supplies, and the result is labelled as such. Do not populate this from general knowledge — a sourced value here would silently become the default for every user.
No default density for diesel. Volume input works only from a density the user supplies.
No default density for kerosene. Volume input works only from a density the user supplies.

No default density for natural gas. Composition varies by network, so a single global value may not be defensible even once sourced — which is an argument for asking the user rather than publishing one. Entering the bill's kilowatt-hours avoids the question entirely.

gwp_sets_note: The 2006 IPCC Guidelines do not publish global warming potential values, so no GWP set in this library may ever be classed 'ipcc'. Vol 1 Ch 4 footnote 3 records that the Guidelines used the Second Assessment Report 100-year GWPs to derive their own key category thresholds and worked examples; that is a statement about the Guidelines' internal arithmetic, not a published GWP table. Vol 1 Ch 8 Annex 2 goes the other way and makes the gap explicit: its reporting tables require the inventory compiler to specify the source of the GWP factors used. Both point at the same conclusion — the choice of GWP set belongs to whoever compiles the inventory, and must be named alongside any CO2-equivalent figure this calculator shows.

gwp_sets.label: IPCC Second Assessment Report (SAR), 100-year
gwp_sets.note: The 2006 IPCC Guidelines do not publish GWP values; this set is external to the methodology. Vol 1 Ch 4 footnote 3 states that the Guidelines used the SAR 100-year GWPs when deriving their own key category thresholds and worked examples, which makes this set the one internally consistent with the Guidelines' own arithmetic. Vol 1 Ch 8 Annex 2 nonetheless requires the compiler to specify the source of the GWP factors used. Source is named at report level only: the exact table reference is not yet confirmed.

gwp_sets.label: IPCC Third Assessment Report (TAR), 100-year
gwp_sets.note: The 2006 IPCC Guidelines do not publish GWP values; this set is external to the methodology. The Guidelines reference TAR GWPs in places, but Vol 1 Ch 4 footnote 3 records that their own key category thresholds and worked examples used the SAR 100-year values, and Vol 1 Ch 8 Annex 2 requires the compiler to specify which source was used. Source is named at report level only: the exact table reference is not yet confirmed.

gwp_sets.label: IPCC Fourth Assessment Report (AR4), 100-year
gwp_sets.note: The 2006 IPCC Guidelines do not publish GWP values; this set is external to the methodology. Vol 1 Ch 4 footnote 3 records that the Guidelines used the SAR 100-year GWPs for their own key category thresholds and worked examples, and Vol 1 Ch 8 Annex 2 requires the compiler to specify the source of the GWP factors used. Source is named at report level only: the exact table reference is not yet confirmed.

gwp_sets.label: IPCC Fifth Assessment Report (AR5), 100-year
gwp_sets.note: The 2006 IPCC Guidelines do not publish GWP values; this set is external to the methodology. Vol 1 Ch 4 footnote 3 records that the Guidelines used the SAR 100-year GWPs for their own key category thresholds and worked examples, and Vol 1 Ch 8 Annex 2 requires the compiler to specify the source of the GWP factors used. AR5 publishes methane GWPs both with and without climate-carbon feedbacks; the figure recorded here is taken to be the value without feedbacks, which is the one used for inventory reporting. Source is named at report level only: the exact table reference is not yet confirmed, and the feedback treatment must be confirmed with it.

gwp_sets.label: IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6), 100-year
gwp_sets.note: The 2006 IPCC Guidelines do not publish GWP values; this set is external to the methodology. Vol 1 Ch 4 footnote 3 records that the Guidelines used the SAR 100-year GWPs for their own key category thresholds and worked examples, and Vol 1 Ch 8 Annex 2 requires the compiler to specify the source of the GWP factors used. AR6 gives two 100-year methane GWPs, a higher one for fossil methane and a lower one for non-fossil methane, so this set carries both rather than an average; fossil_split is true and any consumer must choose by the origin of the fuel burned, which matters directly here because charcoal and firewood are non-fossil. Source is named at report level only: the exact table reference is not yet confirmed.

open_questions: Source fuel densities from a citable authority, so that volume input has a default the user can accept rather than a question they must answer. Asking the user unblocks the input; it does not close this gap.

Confirm with a reviewer that picking the AR6 methane GWP from the fuel's biomass flag is the right rule, now that the engine does so: biomass fuels get the non-fossil value, everything else the fossil one.
Confirm IPCC/IGES copyright position on reproducing default factor tables in a commercial product.

Table 1.1 classifies LPG as a liquid fuel, which is the basis used here, but it is a gas at ambient pressure and a reviewer should say so explicitly before the gross energy path is relied on for it.
